IndusEquip Inc. - Q3 2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the IndusEquip Inc. Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are in listen-only mode. After the presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. To ask a question, you will need to press star one on your telephone keypad. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Sarah Jenkins, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Jenkins (Head of Investor Relations):
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss IndusEquip Inc.'s results for the Q3 2024. Joining me on today's call are Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer; and Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we will be making today are forward-looking in nature and subject to certain risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Mike Thompson.

Mike Thompson (CEO):
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report on IndusEquip Inc.'s performance for the Q3 2024. We've made significant progress on several fronts, and I'd like to highlight a few key achievements. First, we've delivered impressive operating margin expansion across our segments, reflecting the resilience of our diversified portfolio. Second, demand trends remain constructive in our core end markets, including construction, mining, agriculture, and manufacturing, with record backlog levels. Third, our automation and digital offerings continue to accelerate, driving efficiency gains for our customers and high-margin recurring revenue for us. And fourth, our strategic M&A activity is enhancing our technology leadership and market positioning.

We are confident that our strategic initiatives are positioning us for long-term sustainable growth.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Lisa to provide more detail on our financial results.

Lisa Chen (CFO):
Thank you, Mike. Turning to our financial performance, IndusEquip Inc. reported $3.6 billion in revenue for the quarter, representing a 12% increase year-over-year. Gross margin was 38.5%, driven by disciplined pricing, favorable mix, and productivity improvements. Operating expenses were $850 million, resulting in an operating income of $528 million. Our net income for the quarter was $420 million, or $1.85 per share.

We continue to maintain a strong balance sheet, with $1.2 billion in cash and cash equivalents. We are committed to investing in our business to drive future growth and shareholder value.

Thank you, Mike. I'll now dive into our operating margin performance by segment for the third quarter, which reflects the strength of our diversified portfolio amid a volatile industrial landscape. Overall, consolidated operating margins expanded 210 basis points year-over-year to 14.8%, driven by disciplined pricing actions, favorable product mix shifts toward higher-margin aftermarket services, and productivity gains from our Enterprise Lean Sigma program. This marks our sixth consecutive quarter of margin expansion, even as raw material input costs—particularly steel and aluminum—rose 8% sequentially due to lingering supply chain disruptions from the Red Sea rerouting.

Let me break this down by our four core segments: Industrial Automation, Heavy Machinery, Precision Components, and Energy Systems. I'll highlight revenue, margins, key drivers, regional nuances, and strategic levers we're pulling.

Industrial Automation Segment  
Revenue grew 12% year-over-year to $1.2 billion, fueled by strong demand for our next-gen PLCs and collaborative robots, akin to what's powering Rockwell Automation's FactoryTalk ecosystem but with our proprietary AI-edge analytics for predictive maintenance. Operating margins expanded dramatically by 450 basis points to 22.1%—our highest in five years. This was propelled by a 300 bps gross margin lift from supply chain localization in Mexico, reducing lead times by 25% and mitigating tariff exposures under USMCA. Aftermarket services, now 35% of segment revenue (up from 28% last year), delivered 32% margins, benefiting from our Digital Twin platform rollout, which has boosted uptime for customers like automotive OEMs in the EV transition. Regionally, APAC drove 60% of growth with margins at 24%, thanks to pent-up semiconductor fab demand in Taiwan and South Korea, while EMEA margins held steady at 20% despite softer German auto capex. Looking ahead, we're investing $50 million in cobot R&D to capture share in warehouse automation, targeting 25% margins by year-end 2025.

Heavy Machinery Segment  
Here, revenue was flat at $950 million, reflecting softer mining capex amid commodity price volatility—think BHP and Rio Tinto deferring large earthmovers. However, operating margins improved 150 bps to 13.5%, outperforming peers like Caterpillar, which reported similar pressures from diesel engine constraints. Key wins included a 5% price realization on our autonomous haul trucks, plus 200 bps of COGS savings from our Variable Cost Productivity initiative, which optimized weld line capacity utilization to 92% across our Peoria and Monterrey plants. Aftermarket parts mix shifted to 28% of revenue, yielding 18% margins on high-wear components like undercarriage kits. North America was the bright spot at 15% margins, bolstered by data center construction boom driving excavator rentals, while LatAm margins dipped to 11% due to FX headwinds in Brazil (real down 10% YoY). Strategically, we're accelerating electrification pilots—our 100-ton battery-electric dozer prototype secured a $200 million backlog with Fortescue—aiming to add 300 bps to margins via premium pricing and lower lifecycle TCO.

Precision Components Segment  
Revenue surged 18% to $800 million, led by aero aftermarket demand as Boeing and Airbus ramp 737 MAX and A320neo production. Operating margins rose 280 bps to 16.7%, driven by our Aerospace Lean Manufacturing cells, which cut inventory days from 85 to 62 and improved on-time delivery to 98%. Titanium forging costs stabilized post-Ukraine supply shocks, allowing 4% pricing on landing gear struts and turbine blades. Services like our MRO hubs contributed 40% margins, echoing HEICO's model but scaled for industrial turbines too. APAC margins hit 19%, powered by Chinese aero growth and Japanese precision tooling for semis, offsetting EMEA softness at 14% from Airbus strike disruptions. Forward guidance includes $100 million in capex for additive manufacturing lines, positioning us for 20% margins as we penetrate hypersonic programs and wind turbine gearboxes.

Energy Systems Segment  
This segment posted 5% revenue growth to $650 million, with renewables offsetting gas turbine weakness amid Europe's energy transition. Margins expanded 120 bps to 11.2%, below our aspirational 15% but resilient versus GE Vernova's recent dips. Drivers included 15% pricing on solar trackers—our single-axis models now hold 22% U.S. market share—and 150 bps SG&A leverage from shared services. Wind EPC services hit 25% margins on O&M contracts, but hydro equipment faced margin pressure from rare earth magnet shortages. Regionally, North America led at 13% margins with IRA-fueled storage projects, while EMEA improved to 10% post-Nordic offshore wind wins; APAC lagged at 9% due to Australian grid delays. Our strategic pivot: $75 million in hydrogen-ready gas turbine upgrades and microgrid solutions, targeting LNG-to-renewables bridge markets to drive 400 bps margin accretion next year.

In summary, segment margins averaged 15.9% excluding corporates, up 250 bps YoY, with automation and precision leading the charge. Challenges like steel volatility (up 12% QoQ) and labor inflation were offset by 6% productivity gains enterprise-wide. Regionally, North America (45% of revenue) delivered 16.5% margins, APAC 17.2%, EMEA 14.8%, and LatAm 12.1%. For Q4, we guide to 15.2-15.6% consolidated margins, supported by $2.5 billion backlog conversion at 85% and further supply chain de-risking via nearshoring. This positions us well against industry headwinds like potential Section 232 tariffs redux.

Next, let me turn to our demand trends across our core end markets—construction, mining, agriculture, and manufacturing—which collectively represent about 85% of our revenue mix. Overall, we saw robust order intake in the quarter, with total backlog reaching a record $28.5 billion, up 14% year-over-year, driven by strong pricing discipline and share gains in high-margin segments. Book-to-bill came in at 1.25x, signaling continued strength into fiscal 2025. Let me break this down market by market, with regional color and our strategic positioning.

Starting with construction, which accounted for 32% of our Q3 bookings. Demand remains resilient amid a multi-year capex upcycle, fueled by global infrastructure investments. In North America, U.S. highway and bridge projects under the IIJA are accelerating, with our large mining-class excavators and wheel loaders seeing 18% YoY order growth—think our new 988K XE electric wheel loader, which is capturing 25% market share in spec'd fleets for mega-projects like those from Kiewit or Fluor. Housing starts softened to 1.35 million annualized units, pressuring compact equipment, but non-residential construction is up 7%, boosting demand for telehandlers and skid steers. EMEA showed mixed signals: UK and German infra spending lifted dozers by 12%, but French residential weakness led to a 5% dip in backhoe loaders. Asia-Pacific was the standout, with China's urban renewal and India's highway expansions driving 22% growth in our motor graders; we're now shipping over 500 units quarterly to Larsen & Toubro projects. Latin America faced headwinds from Brazilian fiscal tightening, down 8% in aggregates equipment. Strategically, we're leaning into sustainability—our hybrid mini-excavators reduced fleet fuel costs by 30% in pilot programs with Skanska—and telematics adoption hit 65% penetration, unlocking $150 million in recurring aftermarket services. We expect construction orders to grow mid-single digits in Q4, with backlog visibility through H1 2025.

Moving to mining, our highest-margin market at 28% of bookings and 22% operating margins. This segment is on fire, with underground and surface mining equipment orders surging 26% YoY, outpacing peers like Epiroc and Sandvik. Copper and lithium demand for EVs and renewables is the tailwind—global copper mine supply needs to rise 40% by 2030 per Wood Mackenzie, and our autonomous haul trucks are key. In Australia, Roy Hill and BHP expansions ordered 45 of our Cat 793F trucks, contributing to a 35% regional uptick. North America's Nevada gold and copper restarts added 15% growth, while Indonesia's Grasberg mine ramp-up boosted longwall shearers by 20%. South Africa faced labor disruptions, muting coal demand, but our battery-electric underground loaders gained traction with Anglo American, with zero-emission pilots reducing ventilation costs by 25%. Technically, our Command for Hauling system now integrates AI-driven predictive maintenance, cutting downtime 18% and driving 40% attach rates. Pricing held firm at +9%, and aftermarket parts grew 22% on higher utilization. Risks include commodity volatility—iron ore down 12% QoQ—but our exposure is balanced across base metals. Outlook: Double-digit growth persists, supported by $4.2 billion in mining backlog.

Agriculture was softer, representing 18% of bookings and down 4% YoY, reflecting lower farm incomes and delayed equipment cycles. U.S. corn and soy prices fell 15% amid bumper harvests, pushing dealer inventories up 10% and compressing combine and tractor orders. However, precision ag is a bright spot—our AutoPath™ and See & Spray tech on the New Holland CR12.5 harvesters saw 30% adoption, boosting yields 12% in John Deere co-op pilots. Large-acreage row-crop tractors over 300HP held steady at +2%, but compact utility tractors dipped 9% on dairy margin pressures. Brazil's soybean boom countered this, with 25% growth in sprayers and planters; we're ramping production in Piracicaba for CNH synergy. Europe grappled with Ukraine war fallout—wheat prices volatile, but EU CAP subsidies lifted forage equipment 8%. Asia's rice mechanization drove 16% demand for our Kubota-licensed walkers. Strategically, we're investing $200 million in autonomous tractors, with beta tests showing 20% labor savings, and expanding our John Deere-like Financial arm to finance 40% of fleet renewals. We anticipate stabilization in Q4 as inventories normalize, with backlog at $3.8 billion providing a floor.

Finally, manufacturing, 22% of bookings and up 11% YoY, benefiting from reshoring and automation. U.S. CHIPS Act and IRA investments are fueling fab construction—our CNC machining centers and forklifts for Intel and TSMC plants grew 19%. Automotive OEMs like Ford and GM are retooling for EVs, ordering 15% more welding robots and AGVs amid UAW strikes' aftermath. Non-auto factory automation surged on e-commerce; Crown Equipment peers report similar trends. EMEA's battery gigafactories in Hungary and Germany added 14% to our palletizers. China's manufacturing PMI at 49.8 signals caution, but semiconductor capex held our lathes flat. Key initiative: Our Factory 4.0 suite with IoT and edge AI reduced cycle times 22% in Fanuc collaborations. Aftermarket services here grew 16%, with uptime guarantees. Backlog stands at $5.1 billion, with book-to-bill at 1.3x.

In summary, end-market demand is constructive, with mining and manufacturing offsetting ag cyclicality. Regionally, North America (45% of backlog) and APAC (30%) lead, while LatAm lags. We're gaining 150bps share via electrification—20% of new orders are hybrid/electric—and digital services now 18% of revenue, up from 12% two years ago. Margins expanded 220bps to 24.5%, with pricing +7% and cost controls. For FY25, we guide core orders growth of 8-12%, assuming no recession.

As we dive deeper into our Q3 results, I want to spend some time on one of our fastest-growing and highest-margin segments: automation and digital offerings. This area is not just a growth engine for IndusEquip—it's fundamentally transforming how our customers in the manufacturing and industrial equipment space operate, driving efficiency gains that are reshaping their P&Ls and ours.

Let me start with the numbers, which speak for themselves. In Q3, revenue from our automation and digital portfolio grew 28% year-over-year to $178 million, representing 14% of our total segment revenue—up from just 9% a year ago. This marks the sixth straight quarter of double-digit growth, outpacing our core equipment sales by over 15 points. Even more impressively, our digital services—primarily SaaS-based subscriptions via our EquipConnect IoT platform—posted 42% YoY growth, hitting an annualized recurring revenue run-rate of $320 million. Gross margins here are stellar at 78%, a 300-basis-point expansion from last year, thanks to the scalability of cloud-delivered analytics and the shift away from one-time hardware sales.

This isn't hype; it's driven by tangible customer value in an industry hungry for productivity amid persistent labor shortages, supply chain volatility, and the push toward Industry 4.0. Our automation solutions, including collaborative robots (cobots), AI-enabled CNC machines, and edge-computing PLCs, are helping manufacturers boost Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) by an average of 22% within the first 12 months of deployment. For context, that's like adding the equivalent of 15-20% more capacity without new capex—a game-changer when global manufacturing utilization rates are hovering around 75%, per recent McKinsey data.

Let me break down some key technical initiatives fueling this momentum. Our flagship EquipConnect platform, now with over 1.2 million connected assets across 4,500 customer sites, leverages machine learning for predictive maintenance that has reduced unplanned downtime by 35% on average. We're talking real-world MTBF improvements from 1,200 hours to over 2,000 hours on our servo-driven assembly lines. We've integrated generative AI for digital twins—modeled after best-in-class like Siemens' NX or Dassault Systèmes' 3DEXPERIENCE—allowing customers to simulate production scenarios with 95% accuracy, optimizing throughput before a single part is machined.

On the automation front, our next-gen modular AGVs (Automated Guided Vehicles) and AMR (Autonomous Mobile Robots) fleet management system, co-developed with a partnership akin to our collaboration with Rockwell Automation's FactoryTalk ecosystem, saw 45% YoY shipment growth. These aren't basic bots; they're AI-orchestrated swarms that dynamically reroute based on real-time WMS (Warehouse Management System) data, cutting intra-factory logistics costs by 28%. We've also rolled out our EdgeAI controllers, which process 10x more data at the machine level than legacy SCADA systems, enabling zero-latency decisions that have lifted customer throughput rates by 18% in high-mix, low-volume environments like custom industrial machinery.

Regionally, the story is equally compelling. In North America, which accounted for 52% of our digital revenue at $92 million (up 32% YoY), reshoring trends are a tailwind. Automotive OEMs and aerospace players—like those mirroring Ford's or Boeing's smart factory pivots—are snapping up our solutions to counter skilled labor gaps, with the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics projecting a 10% shortfall in manufacturing engineers by 2026. A prime example: a Tier-1 supplier in the Midwest integrated our cobot welders and EquipConnect, slashing cycle times from 45 to 32 seconds per part and improving first-pass yield to 98.5%.

Europe, at 28% of digital revenue ($50 million, +25% YoY), benefits from the EU's Green Deal and re-industrialization push. Our energy-efficient servo motors and AI-optimized HVAC skids align perfectly with carbon reduction mandates, helping chemical processors meet Scope 2 emissions targets while boosting energy efficiency by 24%. In Germany, where factory automation density is the highest globally at 350 robots per 10,000 workers (IFR data), we've gained share against incumbents like ABB and Fanuc.

Asia-Pacific rounded out at 20% ($36 million, +22% YoY), driven by China's "Made in China 2025" and India's PLI schemes. Semiconductor and EV battery makers are deploying our high-precision wafer handling robots, with one major fab in Taiwan reporting a 40% reduction in defect rates via our vision-guided inspection modules.

Strategically, we're doubling down here because the total addressable market for industrial digital twins and automation is exploding—from $15 billion today to $120 billion by 2030, per Gartner forecasts. Our R&D spend in this area is up 35% to $145 million annually, focused on 5G-enabled private networks for ultra-reliable low-latency comms (URLLC) and blockchain for supply chain provenance—critical for traceability in regulated sectors like pharma equipment.

The efficiency flywheel is clear: Customers see rapid ROI—typically 9-12 months payback—leading to 85% renewal rates and 40% upsell penetration. This translates to our P&L via a SaaS-like model: 65% of digital revenue is now recurring, insulating us from cyclical equipment demand. EBITDA margins in the segment hit 42% this quarter, pulling up our overall mix by 150 basis points.

Looking ahead, we expect full-year digital revenue growth of 30-35%, with automation hardware up 25%. Risks like semiconductor shortages persist, but our diversified supply base—40% U.S./EU-sourced—and inventory builds position us well. We're also eyeing M&A, like tuck-ins in AR/VR for remote technician support, to accelerate our edge.

In short, automation and digital aren't silos—they're the connective tissue making our equipment smarter, stickier, and more profitable. This is how IndusEquip is leading the charge in the next era of manufacturing.

Thank you, Mike, and good afternoon, everyone. I'd now like to dive into our M&A activity and the strategic rationale behind it, which continues to be a key pillar of our inorganic growth strategy at IndusEquip Inc. As you know, we've maintained a disciplined approach to capital deployment, targeting bolt-on acquisitions that enhance our core competencies in CNC machining centers, hydraulic forging presses, and automated assembly systems—while delivering compelling ROIC hurdles of at least 15% within three years.

Let me start with the highlights from the quarter. We closed two transformative deals: the $425 million acquisition of Precision Robotics Solutions (PRS) out of Michigan, a leader in AI-enabled collaborative robots or 'cobots' for high-mix, low-volume manufacturing; and the €185 million purchase of Nordic ForgeTech in Sweden, which bolsters our heavy-duty forging capabilities for wind turbine components and EV battery casings. These deals were funded through a mix of cash on hand—$320 million—and $290 million in low-cost term debt at a blended 3.8% rate, preserving our investment-grade balance sheet with net leverage now at 1.8x EBITDA, down from 2.1x pre-announcement.

Financially, these transactions are already tracking ahead of plan. PRS contributed $68 million in trailing twelve-month revenue at a healthy 28% adjusted EBITDA margin, acquired at 11.2x EBITDA—a 25% discount to our peer group comps like Fanuc and ABB, reflecting some near-term supply chain disruptions in their chip sourcing. Nordic ForgeTech added €42 million in sales with 22% margins, bought at 9.8x—a steal given Europe's ongoing steel tariff volatility. Pro forma for these deals, Q3 revenue grew 14% year-over-year to $1.72 billion, with M&A driving 420 basis points of that growth, or about 30% of our total top-line expansion.

Synergies are materializing faster than our initial guide. We're realizing $28 million in run-rate cost savings by year-end, primarily from procurement consolidation—PRS's cobot grippers now leverage our global steel supply chain, shaving 12-15% off component costs—and SG&A overlaps, like shared ERP systems on SAP S/4HANA. Revenue synergies are kicking in too: cross-selling PRS cobots into our existing automotive OEM customer base, including Ford and Stellantis, has already booked $15 million in Q4 orders. We expect these deals to be 8% EPS accretive in FY24, scaling to 12% by FY26, with full integration by mid-next year.

Now, turning to the strategic rationale—this isn't opportunistic M&A; it's a deliberate play to position IndusEquip at the intersection of Industry 4.0 megatrends: automation, electrification, and reshoring. First, technology leadership. PRS gives us proprietary edgeAI software for predictive maintenance, reducing unplanned downtime by up to 35% in welding and assembly lines—critical as manufacturers grapple with labor shortages. Think about it: in a world where McKinsey estimates $1.2 trillion in annual value at stake from predictive analytics alone, we're embedding this into our ModuFlex CNC platforms, which already hold 22% North American market share. We've piloted it with a Tier-1 supplier to Tesla, yielding 18% throughput gains on gigacasting lines.

Second, sustainability and electrification. Nordic ForgeTech's patented hydroforming tech for lightweight aluminum alloys aligns perfectly with the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) and the IRA incentives stateside. Their 95% recyclable forging processes for monopile foundations have us targeting the offshore wind boom—global capacity expected to hit 234 GW by 2028 per IRENA, up 15% CAGR. This diversifies us beyond traditional oil & gas forging, where we've seen 8% volume erosion from OPEC+ cuts.

Regionally, these moves address divergent dynamics. In North America, reshoring is accelerating—U.S. industrial capex up 11% YoY per ISM data—fueled by CHIPS Act fabs and EV battery plants. PRS strengthens our footprint here, where 65% of our cobot installs now target semiconductors, countering ASML and Applied Materials' dominance in photolithography. Europe remains challenged by energy costs—German Ifo Institute pegs manufacturing PMI at 42—but Nordic's low-carbon ops give us a leg up in the Nordics and Benelux, where we're pursuing EPCI contracts for Ørsted-scale wind farms. APAC is our growth engine at 22% YoY organic growth, driven by China's 'Made in China 2025' push into high-end equipment; we're eyeing tuck-ins there to localize servo motor production amid U.S. tariffs.

Broader industry tailwinds validate this strategy. The global industrial machinery market is projected at 6.2% CAGR through 2028 by MarketsandMarkets, propelled by $500 billion in annual automation spend. Competitors like Siemens are paying 14-16x for digital twins bolt-ons, while Rockwell's 12x multiple reflects execution risks—we're trading at 10.5x forward EV/EBITDA, a 20% discount, with M&A set to close that gap. We've also divested a non-core legacy stamping unit for $110 million—1.2x book value—to recycle capital, underscoring our portfolio discipline.

Looking forward, our M&A pipeline is robust: $2-3 billion in dry powder, with three LOIs signed for U.S.-based laser cladding specialists and an Indian precision grinding firm. We'll remain opportunistic but disciplined—no SVB-style overpays—focusing on deals with >20% IRR and adjacency to our $4.1 billion core portfolio. This inorganic flywheel, paired with 9% organic growth guidance, positions us to compound EPS at 12-15% over the cycle.

That concludes my prepared remarks.

Q&A Session:

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question-and-answer session. To ask a question, press star one one. Our first question comes from John Smith with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

John Smith (Goldman Sachs):
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the demand environment you're seeing in the construction market?

Mike Thompson (CEO):
Good morning, John. Absolutely. As Lisa detailed, construction demand remains resilient, making up 32% of our Q3 bookings amid the global infrastructure upcycle. In North America, IIJA projects are accelerating orders for our excavators and electric wheel loaders by 18% year-over-year. APAC is even stronger with 22% growth from China's urban renewal and India's highways. We're seeing mid-single-digit growth expected in Q4, supported by sustainability plays like our hybrid excavators and strong telematics uptake.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Carter with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Emily Carter (JPMorgan):
What are your expectations for capital expenditures in the coming year?

Lisa Chen (CFO):
Thanks, Emily. For FY25, we're guiding capex to $450-500 million, up slightly from this year. This includes $100 million for additive manufacturing in precision components, $75 million for energy systems upgrades like hydrogen-ready turbines, $50 million in cobot R&D for automation, and the balance for productivity initiatives across plants. This supports our margin expansion to 15.2-15.6% in Q4 and beyond, while maintaining ROIC above 15%.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Robert Lee with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Robert Lee (Morgan Stanley):
How are you managing supply chain disruptions, and what impact are they having on your margins?

Mike Thompson (CEO):
Good question, Robert. Supply chain issues, like Red Sea rerouting pushing steel and aluminum costs up 8% sequentially, are real, but we've offset them effectively. Localization in Mexico cut lead times 25% in automation, and our Variable Cost Productivity program hit 92% capacity utilization in heavy machinery. Enterprise-wide, 6% productivity gains and nearshoring have driven 210 bps consolidated margin expansion to 14.8%, with automation at 22.1%. Margins are resilient, and our $28.5 billion backlog provides visibility.

Closing Remarks:

Mike Thompson (CEO):
Thank you for your questions and your interest in IndusEquip Inc. We are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our strategy and delivering long-term value for our shareholders.

Sarah Jenkins (Head of Investor Relations):
Thank you, everyone, for joining us today. This concludes our earnings call. Have a great day.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
